title: Define an algorithm. Write any four characteristics of a good algorithm.
answer_html:
An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure or set of rules to be followed in calculations or other problem-solving operations. Characteristics:

  • Finiteness: Must terminate after a finite number of steps.
  • Definiteness: Each step must be precisely defined.
  • Input: Has zero or more inputs.
  • Output: Produces one or more outputs.
  • Effectiveness: Operations must be basic enough to be done exactly and in finite time.

title: Define algorithm correctness. Differentiate between partial correctness and total correctness with suitable examples.
answer_html:
Algorithm Correctness: An algorithm is correct if, for every valid input, it halts and produces the correct output as defined by its specifications.

  • Partial Correctness: If the algorithm halts, it produces the correct output (but it might not halt). Example: A while(true) loop that searches for an element and breaks when found. If the element isn't there, it might loop forever.
  • Total Correctness: The algorithm is guaranteed to halt, and when it halts, it produces the correct output. Example: A standard for-loop based linear search that scans an array from start to end and returns true/false.

A loop invariant is a condition or property that is true before and after each iteration of a loop. It is used to prove the correctness of loop structures.

  1. Initialization: The invariant must be true before the first iteration of the loop.
  2. Maintenance: If it is true before an iteration of the loop, it remains true before the next iteration.
  3. Termination: When the loop terminates, the invariant gives us a useful property that helps show the algorithm is correct.

title: Explain how loop invariants can be used to prove the correctness of a sorting algorithm.
answer_html:
In sorting algorithms like Insertion Sort, a loop invariant can be defined as: 'At the start of each iteration i, the subarray A[0...i-1] consists of the elements originally in A[0...i-1], but in sorted order.'

  • Initialization: For i=1, A[0] is just a single element, which is trivially sorted.
  • Maintenance: During iteration i, the algorithm inserts A[i] into its correct position in A[0...i-1], making A[0...i] sorted.
  • Termination: The loop ends when i = n. The invariant states that A[0...n-1] is sorted, which means the entire array is sorted, proving correctness.

title: Define the Divide and Conquer paradigm. Explain its three basic steps with a suitable example.
answer_html:
Divide and Conquer Paradigm

The Divide and Conquer paradigm is an algorithmic design strategy that solves a problem by recursively breaking it down into two or more sub-problems of the same or related type, until these become simple enough to be solved directly. The solutions to the sub-problems are then combined to give a solution to the original problem.

It consists of three basic steps:

  • Divide: Break the given problem into smaller sub-problems.
  • Conquer: Recursively solve these sub-problems. If the sub-problem size is small enough, solve it directly (base case).
  • Combine: Merge the solutions of the sub-problems to form the solution of the original problem.
Example: Merge Sort

In Merge Sort:

  • Divide: Divide the unsorted array of size n into two sub-arrays of size n/2.
  • Conquer: Recursively sort the two sub-arrays using Merge Sort.
  • Combine: Merge the two sorted sub-arrays into a single sorted array.

Quick Recall:

  • Divide: Break the given problem into smaller sub-problems.
  • Conquer: Recursively solve these sub-problems. If the sub-problem size is small enough, solve it directly (base case).
  • Combine: Merge the solutions of the sub-problems to form the solution of the original problem.

  • Divide: This step involves breaking the original problem into a set of smaller sub-problems. The sub-problems should represent a smaller instance of the same original problem.

title: Explain the general structure of a Divide and Conquer algorithm. How is it different from an iterative algorithm?
answer_html:
General Structure

The general structure of a Divide and Conquer algorithm can be represented recursively:

Algorithm DAndC(P)
{
    if Small(P) then
        return S(P); // Solve directly
    else
    {
        Divide P into smaller instances P1, P2, ..., Pk, k ≥ 1;
        Apply DAndC to each of these subproblems;
        return Combine(DAndC(P1), DAndC(P2), ..., DAndC(Pk));
    }
}
Difference from Iterative Algorithms
  • Control Flow: Divide and Conquer algorithms rely heavily on recursion (functions calling themselves), whereas iterative algorithms use loops (for, while) to repeat tasks.
  • State Management: In recursion, state is maintained implicitly by the call stack. In iteration, variables explicitly hold state (like loop counters).
  • Approach: Divide and conquer works top-down (breaking large to small), while dynamic programming or iterative methods can work bottom-up (solving small to build large).

title: What is a recurrence relation? Explain its role in analyzing the time complexity of recursive algorithms.
answer_html:
A recurrence relation is an equation or inequality that describes a mathematical function in terms of its value on smaller inputs.

Role in Analyzing Time Complexity:

When an algorithm contains a recursive call, its running time can be described by a recurrence relation. For example, in Merge Sort, solving a problem of size n involves two subproblems of size n/2, and merging takes linear time O(n). This gives the recurrence:

T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)

By solving this recurrence relation (using methods like the Substitution Method, Recursion Tree Method, or Master Theorem), we can express the time complexity of the algorithm in Big-O notation (e.g., O(n log n)).

title: Solve the following recurrence using the substitution method: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n
answer_html:
Recurrence: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n

Guess: T(n) = O(n log n). We need to prove that T(n) ≤ c · n log n for some constant c > 0.

Proof by induction:

  • Assume the bound holds for n/2, i.e., T(n/2) ≤ c · (n/2) log(n/2).
  • Substitute this into the recurrence:
    T(n) ≤ 2 · [c · (n/2) log(n/2)] + n
    T(n) ≤ c · n log(n/2) + n
    T(n) ≤ c · n(log n - log 2) + n
    T(n) ≤ c · n log n - c · n + n
  • We want T(n) ≤ c · n log n. This holds true if:
    c · n log n - c · n + n ≤ c · n log n
    -c · n + n ≤ 0
    c ≥ 1

Since we can choose c ≥ 1, the guess is correct.

Result: T(n) = O(n log n)

title: Explain the best-case, average-case, and worst-case time complexity of Quick Sort.
answer_html:
Best Case: O(n log n)

Occurs when the pivot chosen at each step divides the array into two roughly equal halves. The recursion tree has a depth of log(n) and partitioning at each level takes O(n) time. Recurrence: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)

Average Case: O(n log n)

Occurs when the pivot randomly divides the array into proportional splits (e.g., 9-to-1 split or 3-to-1 split). Even an unbalanced split like 99-to-1 results in an O(n log n) running time, as the depth of the tree is bounded by a logarithmic function.

Worst Case: O(n²)

Occurs when the pivot is consistently the smallest or largest element, leading to completely unbalanced partitions (one sub-array of size n-1, and one of size 0). This creates a skewed recursion tree of depth n. Example: sorting an already sorted array when the first or last element is chosen as the pivot. Recurrence: T(n) = T(n-1) + O(n)

title: Explain how the Divide and Conquer technique can be used for multiplication of large integers.
answer_html:
When integers are very large (e.g., hundreds of digits in cryptography), standard multiplication (O(n²)) is too slow. The Divide and Conquer technique (Karatsuba algorithm) speeds this up.

Process:

  1. Divide: Split each n-digit number into two halves (high and low parts).
    Example: X = A*10^(n/2) + B and Y = C*10^(n/2) + D
  2. Standard Divide and Conquer: Compute four partial products (AC, AD, BC, BD). This yields T(n) = 4T(n/2) + O(n) → O(n²).
  3. Karatsuba Optimization: Compute only three products recursively:
    • P1 = A * C
    • P2 = B * D
    • P3 = (A + B) * (C + D)
    The middle term (AD + BC) is derived as P3 - P1 - P2.
  4. Conquer and Combine: This reduces the recurrence to T(n) = 3T(n/2) + O(n), improving the time complexity to O(nlog23) ≈ O(n1.585).

title: Define an algorithm and state characteristics of a good algorithm.
answer_html:
An algorithm is a finite, well-defined sequence of unambiguous computational steps that takes some value or set of values as input and produces some value or set of values as output.

Key characteristics of a good algorithm are:

  • Input & Output: Takes zero or more well-defined inputs and produces at least one clearly defined output.
  • Definiteness: Each step is clear, precise, and unambiguous.
  • Finiteness: Must terminate after a finite number of steps for all valid inputs.
  • Effectiveness: Operations must be basic enough to be carried out exactly and in a finite length of time.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: A finite step-by-step procedure converting input to output. Criteria: Input, Output, Definiteness (unambiguous), Finiteness (terminates), and Effectiveness (feasible).

title: Define algorithm correctness.
answer_html:
An algorithm is said to be correct if, for every valid instance of the input, it halts (terminates) and produces the correct and expected output according to the problem specification.

Algorithm correctness involves two distinct proofs:

  • Partial Correctness: If the algorithm terminates, the output produced satisfies the post-conditions.
  • Total Correctness: The algorithm is guaranteed to terminate and the final output satisfies the post-conditions.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: An algorithm is correct if it terminates for all valid inputs and produces the specified output. Proven via partial correctness + termination.

title: Define the divide-and-conquer paradigm.
answer_html:
The Divide-and-Conquer paradigm is an algorithmic design strategy based on multi-branched recursion that solves a problem through three essential steps:

  1. Divide: Partition the original problem into two or more smaller, disjoint subproblems of the same type.
  2. Conquer: Solve the subproblems recursively. If subproblems are small enough (base case), solve them directly.
  3. Combine: Merge the solutions of the subproblems into a comprehensive solution for the original problem.

Examples: Merge Sort, Quick Sort, Binary Search, Strassen's Matrix Multiplication.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: Divide into smaller subproblems -> Conquer recursively (or base case) -> Combine sub-solutions into the final result (e.g., Merge Sort, Quick Sort).

title: Define dynamic programming.
answer_html:
Dynamic Programming (DP) is an algorithm design technique used for solving optimization problems by breaking them down into simpler, overlapping subproblems, solving each subproblem once, and storing its solution in a table (memoization or tabulation) to avoid redundant recalculations.

Two fundamental prerequisites for applying Dynamic Programming are:

  • Optimal Substructure: An optimal solution to the problem contains within it optimal solutions to its subproblems.
  • Overlapping Subproblems: The recursive formulation revisits the same subproblems repeatedly rather than generating new ones.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: Solves optimization problems by storing solutions to overlapping subproblems to avoid recomputation. Requires: Optimal Substructure and Overlapping Subproblems.

title: Define backtracking.
answer_html:
Backtracking is a systematic, algorithmic search technique that builds candidates for a solution incrementally and abandons ("backtracks" from) a candidate as soon as it determines that the candidate cannot possibly be extended to a valid or optimal solution.

  • It traverses the problem's State-Space Tree typically using Depth-First Search (DFS).
  • When a dead end or constraint violation is encountered at a non-promising node, the search prunes that branch and retreats to the parent node to explore alternative choices.
  • Examples: N-Queens Problem, Subset Sum Problem, Graph Coloring, Hamiltonian Cycle.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: A depth-first search of the state space tree that abandons (backtracks from) paths as soon as constraints are violated. Prunes dead ends to find valid solutions (e.g., N-Queens).

title: What is pseudocode? State two advantages of using pseudocode.
answer_html:
Pseudocode is an informal, high-level description of the operating principles of an algorithm. It uses the structural conventions of normal programming languages but is intended for human reading rather than machine execution.

Two key advantages of pseudocode are:

  • Language Independence: It allows algorithm designers to articulate logical solutions without getting bogged down in syntax constraints, memory management, or compiler specifics of languages like C++, Java, or Python.
  • Ease of Analysis & Translation: It facilitates formal asymptotic analysis (counting steps, loops, and conditions) and can be easily translated into any target programming language.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: High-level informal algorithmic code for human reading. Advantages: Language-independent (no strict syntax) and easy to translate into real programming code.

title: Arrange the following functions in increasing order of growth: (n log n, n log n^2, n^2).
answer_html:
To arrange $n \log n$, $n \log(n^2)$, and $n^2$ in increasing order of asymptotic growth:

  1. Simplify $n \log(n^2)$: Using logarithmic identity $\log(a^b) = b \log a$:$$n \log(n^2) = n \cdot (2 \log n) = 2 n \log n$$
  2. Compare $n \log n$ and $n \log(n^2)$: Both have the exact same asymptotic growth rate: $\Theta(n \log n)$. Asymptotically, $n \log n = \Theta(n \log(n^2))$.
  3. Compare with $n^2$: Dividing $n^2$ by $n \log n$ as $n \to \infty$:$$\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{n \log n}{n^2} = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{\log n}{n} = 0$$Hence, $n^2$ grows strictly faster than $n \log n$ and $n \log(n^2)$.

Increasing Order of Growth:

$$\mathbf{n \log n \le n \log(n^2) < n^2} \quad \text{or} \quad \mathbf{n \log n \sim 2n \log n < n^2}$$
simplified_html: Quick Recall: $n \log(n^2) = 2n \log n$. Both $n \log n$ and $2n \log n$ belong to $\Theta(n \log n)$. Quadratic $n^2$ grows much faster. Order: $n \log n \le n \log(n^2) < n^2$.

title: State the purpose of a loop invariant. Why it is used
answer_html:
A Loop Invariant is a formal logical predicate/property about the algorithm's state that is true before the first iteration of a loop, remains true before and after every subsequent iteration, and remains true upon loop termination.

Why it is used:

  • Proving Correctness: It serves as a mathematical proof technique (analogous to mathematical induction) to formally verify that an iterative algorithm correctly achieves its intended outcome.
  • Three Required Proof Steps:
    1. Initialization: True prior to the first loop iteration (base case).
    2. Maintenance: If true before an iteration, it remains true before the next iteration (inductive step).
    3. Termination: When the loop terminates, the invariant provides a useful property that helps prove the algorithm is correct.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: A condition that remains true before, during, and after a loop. Used to formally prove algorithm correctness via Initialization, Maintenance, and Termination.

title: What is a recurrence relation? How it can be solved?
answer_html:
A Recurrence Relation is an equation or inequality that defines a function $T(n)$ in terms of its values on smaller inputs (e.g., $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)$). In computer science, they describe the execution time of recursive algorithms.

Major Methods to Solve Recurrence Relations:

  1. Substitution Method: Guess the form of the mathematical solution and then use mathematical induction to find the constants and verify the solution.
  2. Recursion Tree Method: Visualizes the recurrence as a tree of recursive calls where nodes represent the cost incurred at each level; summing the costs across all levels yields the total cost.
  3. Master Theorem Method: A cookbook formula that provides instantaneous asymptotic solutions for recurrences of the form $T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n)$ by comparing $f(n)$ with $n^{\log_b a}$.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: An equation expressing $T(n)$ using smaller inputs (e.g., $T(n/2)$). Solved via: (1) Substitution Method (guess + induction), (2) Recursion Tree (sum levels), (3) Master Method (formula for $aT(n/b) + f(n)$).

title: Solve T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n using the Master Method.
answer_html:
Given Recurrence: $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n$.

Step 1: Identify Parameters:

  • Form: $T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n)$
  • $a = 2$, $b = 2$, and $f(n) = n$.

Step 2: Calculate Critical Exponent $n^{\log_b a}$:

$$n^{\log_b a} = n^{\log_2 2} = n^1 = n$$

Step 3: Compare $f(n)$ with $n^{\log_b a}$:

  • Here, $f(n) = n$ and $n^{\log_b a} = n$.
  • Since $f(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_b a}) = \Theta(n)$, this corresponds strictly to Case 2 of the Master Theorem with $k = 0$.

Step 4: Apply Case 2 Formula:

$$T(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_b a} \log^{k+1} n) = \Theta(n^1 \log^1 n) = \mathbf{\Theta(n \log n)}$$

Conclusion: The solution to the recurrence is $\mathbf{\Theta(n \log n)}$ (the characteristic complexity of Merge Sort).
simplified_html: Quick Recall: $a=2, b=2, f(n)=n$. $n^{\log_2 2} = n$. Since $f(n) = \Theta(n)$, Master Theorem Case 2 applies: $T(n) = \mathbf{\Theta(n \log n)}$.

title: What is the principle of optimality? Explain in detail
answer_html:
The Principle of Optimality (originally formulated by Richard Bellman) states that:

"An optimal policy has the property that whatever the initial state and initial decision are, the remaining decisions must constitute an optimal policy with regard to the state resulting from the first decision."

In algorithmic terms, a problem satisfies the principle of optimality (also called Optimal Substructure) if an optimal solution to the overall problem can be constructed efficiently from optimal solutions to its constituent subproblems.

Significance:

  • It is the foundational theoretical requirement for both Dynamic Programming and Greedy Algorithms.
  • Valid Example: Shortest Path in Graphs. If the shortest path from $A$ to $C$ passes through $B$, then the sub-path from $A$ to $B$ must also be the shortest path between $A$ and $B$.
  • Counter-Example: Longest Simple Path in general graphs does NOT satisfy the principle of optimality (cannot compose independently).
simplified_html: Quick Recall: An optimal solution to a problem contains optimal solutions to its subproblems. Necessary prerequisite for Dynamic Programming and Greedy algorithms (e.g., shortest paths).

title: Calculate C(8,5) using the binomial-coefficient formula.
answer_html:
Binomial Coefficient Recurrence Formula (Pascal's Identity):

$$C(n, k) = C(n-1, k-1) + C(n-1, k) \quad \text{with base cases } C(n, 0) = C(n, n) = 1$$

Factorial Formula:

$$C(n, k) = \frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}$$

Step-by-Step Calculation for $C(8, 5)$:

$$C(8, 5) = \frac{8!}{5!(8-5)!} = \frac{8!}{5! \times 3!}$$

Expanding and cancelling $5!$:

$$C(8, 5) = \frac{8 \times 7 \times 6 \times 5!}{5! \times (3 \times 2 \times 1)} = \frac{8 \times 7 \times 6}{6} = 8 \times 7 = \mathbf{56}$$

Note: In Dynamic Programming, $C(n, k)$ is computed iteratively using an $(n+1) \times (k+1)$ table in $O(n k)$ time without encountering large factorial integer overflow.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: $C(8, 5) = \frac{8!}{5! \times 3!} = \frac{8 \times 7 \times 6}{6} = \mathbf{56}$. In DP, Pascal's triangle table computes $C(n, k)$ in $O(nk)$ time without factorial overflow.

title: Explain N-Queens problem.
answer_html:
The N-Queens Problem is a classic combinatorial constraint satisfaction problem that requires placing $N$ non-attacking chess queens on an $N \times N$ chessboard such that no two queens threaten each other.

According to chess rules, two queens attack each other if they share:

  1. The same row.
  2. The same column.
  3. The same diagonal (both major and minor diagonals).

Mathematical Formulation:

  • Represent solution as an array X[1..N] where X[i] denotes the column index of the queen placed in row i.
  • Row and column attacks are avoided by ensuring X[i] != X[j] for all $i \neq j$.
  • Diagonal attacks are avoided by ensuring: $|X[i] - X[j]| \neq |i - j|$.

It has no solution for $N=2$ and $N=3$. The smallest non-trivial solution is for $N=4$ (has 2 distinct solutions).
simplified_html: Quick Recall: Place $N$ queens on an $N \times N$ board so no two share the same row, column, or diagonal ($|X[i]-X[j]| \neq |i-j|$). Solved via Backtracking DFS.

title: Explain backtracking in the N-Queens problem.
answer_html:
Applying Backtracking to the N-Queens Problem avoids exploring all $N^N$ brute-force configurations by pruning non-promising paths:

  1. Incremental Placement: Queens are placed one by one in successive rows (starting with row 1).
  2. Bounding / Safety Check (Place(k, i)): Before placing queen $k$ in column $i$, check if column $i$ or either diagonal is already occupied by any queen $j < k$:$$\text{Conflict if } X[j] == i \quad \text{OR} \quad |X[j] - i| == |j - k|$$
  3. Pruning & Retreat: If no column in row $k$ is safe (dead end), the algorithm terminates exploration of the entire sub-tree beneath this node and backtracks to row $k-1$ to reposition the previous queen.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: Places queens row-by-row. Before placing, checks column and diagonal conflicts. If a row has no safe column, prunes the sub-tree and backtracks to reposition the queen in the previous row.

title: Explain Big-O, Big-Ω and Big-Θ notation with examples.
answer_html:
The three fundamental asymptotic notations used to bound algorithm running time:

  1. Big-O Notation ($O$ - Asymptotic Upper Bound):$$f(n) = O(g(n)) \iff \exists c > 0, n_0 > 0 \text{ such that } 0 \le f(n) \le c \cdot g(n) \quad \forall n \ge n_0$$Represents the worst-case ceiling. Example: $3n + 5 = O(n)$ (with $c = 4, n_0 = 5$).
  2. Big-Omega Notation ($\Omega$ - Asymptotic Lower Bound):$$f(n) = \Omega(g(n)) \iff \exists c > 0, n_0 > 0 \text{ such that } 0 \le c \cdot g(n) \le f(n) \quad \forall n \ge n_0$$Represents the best-case floor. Example: $2n^2 - 3n = \Omega(n^2)$ (with $c = 1, n_0 = 3$).
  3. Big-Theta Notation ($\Theta$ - Asymptotically Tight Bound):$$f(n) = \Theta(g(n)) \iff \exists c_1, c_2 > 0, n_0 > 0 \text{ such that } 0 \le c_1 \cdot g(n) \le f(n) \le c_2 \cdot g(n) \quad \forall n \ge n_0$$Sandwiches $f(n)$ from both above and below. Holds if and only if $f(n) = O(g(n))$ and $f(n) = \Omega(g(n))$. Example: $6n^2 + 4n = \Theta(n^2)$.
simplified_html:
Quick Recall:

  • Big-O ($O$): Upper bound / worst-case ceiling ($f(n) \le c \cdot g(n)$).
  • Big-Omega ($\Omega$): Lower bound / best-case floor ($f(n) \ge c \cdot g(n)$).
  • Big-Theta ($\Theta$): Tight bound sandwiched between constants ($c_1 g(n) \le f(n) \le c_2 g(n)$).

title: Explain the aggregate method of amortized analysis.
answer_html:
In Amortized Analysis, the average running time of an operation over a worst-case sequence of $n$ operations is computed, guaranteeing that the average cost per operation is small even if an occasional single operation is expensive.

The Aggregate Method:

  • In the aggregate method, we determine the total worst-case cost $T(n)$ for an entire sequence of $n$ operations.
  • The amortized cost per operation is then directly computed as:$$\text{Amortized Cost} = \frac{T(n)}{n}$$
  • Every operation in the sequence is assigned the same identical amortized cost, regardless of whether it was cheap or expensive.
  • Classic Example: Dynamic Array Resizing. Appending $n$ items triggers occasional array doubling ($1 + 2 + 4 + \dots + n = 2n$ copy cost) plus $n$ simple inserts. Total cost $T(n) \le 3n$. Amortized cost per append $= \frac{3n}{n} = O(1)$.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: Finds the total worst-case time $T(n)$ for a sequence of $n$ operations and divides by $n$ ($\text{Cost} = T(n)/n$). Assigns every operation the same average cost (e.g., dynamic array append is amortized $O(1)$).

title: Sort 42, 17, 8, 31, 23, 5 using Selection Sort. Show the array after each pass.
answer_html:
Selection Sort Algorithm: Repeatedly finds the minimum element from the unsorted subarray and swaps it with the first element of the unsorted subarray.

Initial Array: [42, 17, 8, 31, 23, 5] ($n = 6$)

    Array: [5, 17, 8, 31, 23, 42]
  2. Pass 2: Find minimum in index 1..5. Minimum is 8 (at index 2). Swap with A[1]=17.
    Array: [5, 8, 17, 31, 23, 42]
  3. Pass 3: Find minimum in index 2..5. Minimum is 17 (at index 2). Already in place, no swap.
    Array: [5, 8, 17, 31, 23, 42]
  4. Pass 4: Find minimum in index 3..5. Minimum is 23 (at index 4). Swap with A[3]=31.
    Array: [5, 8, 17, 23, 31, 42]
  5. Pass 5: Find minimum in index 4..5. Minimum is 31 (at index 4). Already in place, no swap.
    Array: [5, 8, 17, 23, 31, 42]

Final Sorted Array: [5, 8, 17, 23, 31, 42] (Total 5 passes, Time Complexity $\Theta(n^2)$).
simplified_html: Quick Recall: Each pass finds the minimum unsorted item and swaps it into place. Pass 1: swaps (42,5); Pass 2: swaps (17,8); Pass 3: 17 stays; Pass 4: swaps (31,23); Pass 5: 31 stays. Result: [5, 8, 17, 23, 31, 42].

Item $i$ ($w_i, p_i$)$w=0$$w=1$$w=2$$w=3$$w=4$$w=5$

title: For matrix dimensions of three matrices are : [5×3, 3×6, 6×5], calculate the scalar multiplication costs of (A1(A2.A3) and (A1.A2)A3). Identify the better parenthesization.
answer_html:
Given Dimensions: $A_1 = 5 \times 3$, $A_2 = 3 \times 6$, $A_3 = 6 \times 5$. ($p_0 = 5, p_1 = 3, p_2 = 6, p_3 = 5$)

Multiplying a matrix of size $p \times q$ by $q \times r$ requires $p \times q \times r$ scalar multiplications.

Case 1: Parenthesization $((A_1 \cdot A_2) \cdot A_3)$:

  1. Cost of $(A_1 \cdot A_2)$: Size is $5 \times 6$.$$\text{Cost}_1 = 5 \times 3 \times 6 = 90 \text{ multiplications}$$
  2. Cost of multiplying result $(A_1 A_2)$ by $A_3$ ($5 \times 6$ with $6 \times 5$):$$\text{Cost}_2 = 5 \times 6 \times 5 = 150 \text{ multiplications}$$
  3. Total Cost: $90 + 150 = \mathbf{240} \text{ multiplications}$.

Case 2: Parenthesization $(A_1 \cdot (A_2 \cdot A_3))$:

  1. Cost of $(A_2 \cdot A_3)$: Size is $3 \times 5$.$$\text{Cost}_1 = 3 \times 6 \times 5 = 90 \text{ multiplications}$$

title: Explain the Max-Min algorithm using the divide-and-conquer approach.
answer_html:
The Max-Min Divide-and-Conquer Algorithm simultaneously finds the maximum and minimum elements in an array of size $n$ using significantly fewer comparisons than brute-force.

Algorithmic Strategy:

  1. Base Case 1 ($n = 1$): If array has 1 element: $\min = \max = A[1]$ (0 comparisons).
  2. Base Case 2 ($n = 2$): If array has 2 elements: Compare $A[1]$ and $A[2]$, assign $\max$ and $\min$ (1 comparison).
  3. Recursive Step ($n > 2$): Divide array into two halves at midpoint $mid = (low + high) / 2$. Recursively find $(\min_1, \max_1)$ for left half and $(\min_2, \max_2)$ for right half. Combine:$$\min = \min(\min_1, \min_2), \quad \max = \max(\max_1, \max_2)$$

Comparison Count Recurrence:

$$T(n) = 2T(n/2) + 2 \implies T(n) = \frac{3n}{2} - 2 \text{ comparisons}$$

Compared to straightforward linear search which takes $2n - 2$ comparisons, the Divide-and-Conquer approach saves 25% of comparison operations.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: Splits array into halves. Recursively finds min and max of each half, then combines in 2 comparisons. Total comparisons: $\frac{3n}{2} - 2$ (25% fewer than linear search's $2n-2$).

title: What is the basic principle of Selection Sort?
answer_html:
The basic working principle of Selection Sort is: in each pass through the array, it scans the remaining unsorted subarray to select the minimum element, and swaps it with the element at the beginning of the unsorted subarray.

This incrementally expands the sorted prefix by one element per pass until the entire array is sorted in $O(n^2)$ time using $O(1)$ auxiliary memory.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: Scans unsorted section for minimum element, swaps it to the front, and repeats. $O(n^2)$ time and $O(1)$ space.

title: What is the role of a pivot in Quick Sort?
answer_html:
The pivot in Quick Sort acts as a reference partitioning element around which the array is rearranged such that:

  • All elements smaller than or equal to the pivot are placed to its left.
  • All elements strictly greater than the pivot are placed to its right.
  • The pivot itself settles into its final, permanent sorted position in the array without requiring further movement.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: A benchmark element that partitions the array: smaller items go left, larger items go right, placing the pivot into its final sorted index.

title: Define overlapping subproblems.
answer_html:
A problem exhibits Overlapping Subproblems if a recursive algorithm solves the exact same smaller subproblems repeatedly, rather than generating brand-new subproblems at each step.

Example: In computing Fibonacci numbers recursively ($F(n) = F(n-1) + F(n-2)$), $F(n-2)$ and $F(n-3)$ are recalculated exponentially many times. Dynamic programming saves solutions to overlapping subproblems in memory tables, reducing running time from exponential $O(2^n)$ to linear $O(n)$.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: When identical subproblems are solved repeatedly in a recursion tree (e.g., Fibonacci). DP caches these results to avoid exponential recalculation.

title: What is the minimax principle?
answer_html:
The Minimax Principle is a decision rule used in two-player zero-sum adversarial games (e.g., Chess, Tic-Tac-Toe):

  • The maximizing player seeks a strategy that maximizes their minimum possible payoff (maximizing the worst-case return).
  • The minimizing player seeks a move that minimizes the opponent's maximum gain.
  • It assumes both players play optimally, evaluating board state values from the leaf nodes back to the root of the game tree.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: Decision rule for 2-player games: Maximize your minimum payoff assuming the opponent plays to minimize your score.

title: In what cases amortized analysis should be used ?
answer_html:
Amortized Analysis should be used when:

  • An algorithm occasionally executes an expensive, high-cost operation, but that expensive operation is guaranteed to occur very infrequently.
  • The expensive operation is preceded by or pays for a large sequence of cheap, constant-time operations.
  • Traditional worst-case analysis of a single step produces an overly pessimistic bound that misrepresents the true efficiency of a sequence of operations.
  • Classic Examples: Dynamic array capacity doubling, Fibonacci heap operations, splay trees, and disjoint-set (Union-Find) structures.

title: Explain the role of the partitioning step in Quick Sort. How does it divide an array?
answer_html:
The partitioning step is the core engine of Quick Sort. Its role is to arrange elements in linear $O(n)$ time around a chosen pivot element:

  1. Pivot Selection: A pivot is chosen (e.g., first, last, median, or random element).
  2. Two-Pointer Rearrangement: Scans array using two pointers (Lomuto or Hoare scheme):
    • Elements smaller than the pivot are moved into the left partition.
    • Elements larger than the pivot are moved into the right partition.
  3. Pivot Placement: The pivot is swapped into the boundary between the two partitions.
  4. Division: The array is divided into two independent subproblems: $A[p..q-1]$ and $A[q+1..r]$. Crucially, unlike Merge Sort, no combine step is required because the pivot is already in its final position.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: Rearranges elements in $O(n)$ time so smaller elements are to the left of the pivot and larger elements to the right. The pivot reaches its final sorted spot, leaving two independent sub-arrays.

title: Using denominations 3, 2, 1, find the coins selected by dynamic programming for amount 5.

DP Array Construction:

  • $dp[0] = 0$
  • $dp[1] = 1 + dp[0] = 1$ (coin 1)
  • $dp[2] = 1 + \min(dp[1], dp[0]) = 1 + 0 = 1$ (coin 2)
  • $dp[3] = 1 + \min(dp[2], dp[1], dp[0]) = 1 + 0 = 1$ (coin 3)
  • $dp[4] = 1 + \min(dp[3], dp[2], dp[1]) = 1 + \min(1, 1, 1) = 2$ (coins 2+2 or 3+1)
  • $dp[5] = 1 + \min(dp[4], dp[3], dp[2]) = 1 + \min(2, 1, 1) = 1 + 1 = \mathbf{2}$

Coins Selected for Amount 5:

  • Trace back from $dp[5]$: using coin 3 leads to $dp[2]$ (which uses coin 2).
  • Selected Coins: {3, 2} (Total 2 coins: $3 + 2 = 5$).
simplified_html: Quick Recall: DP builds min coins for amounts 0 to 5. Minimum coins required for amount 5 is 2 coins (using denominations 3 and 2).

title: Find Big O notation for the following functions: a. f(n) = 2n + 6n^2 + 3n, b. f(n) = 4n^3 + 2n + 3.
answer_html:
a. Analysis for $f(n) = 2n + 6n^2 + 3n$:

  1. Combine like linear terms: $f(n) = 6n^2 + 5n$.
  2. Identify the dominant term: As $n \to \infty$, the quadratic term $6n^2$ dominates the linear term $5n$.
  3. Drop lower-order terms and leading coefficients:$$f(n) \le 6n^2 + 5n^2 = 11n^2 \quad \forall n \ge 1$$
  4. By formal definition with $c = 11$ and $n_0 = 1$:$$\mathbf{f(n) = O(n^2)}$$

b. Analysis for $f(n) = 4n^3 + 2n + 3$:

  1. Identify the highest-degree term: The cubic term $4n^3$ grows asymptotically faster than $2n$ and constant $3$.
  2. For all $n \ge 1$:$$4n^3 + 2n + 3 \le 4n^3 + 2n^3 + 3n^3 = 9n^3$$
  3. By formal definition with $c = 9$ and $n_0 = 1$:$$\mathbf{f(n) = O(n^3)}$$
simplified_html: Quick Recall: (a) $6n^2 + 5n$ is dominated by $n^2 \implies \mathbf{O(n^2)}$. (b) $4n^3 + 2n + 3$ is dominated by $n^3 \implies \mathbf{O(n^3)}$.

title: Compare the growth rates of n log n and n^2 for large values of n.
answer_html:
To compare the asymptotic growth rates of $f(n) = n \log n$ and $g(n) = n^2$, evaluate the limit of their ratio as $n \to \infty$:

$$\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{f(n)}{g(n)} = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{n \log n}{n^2} = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{\log n}{n}$$

Applying L'Hôpital's Rule (differentiating numerator and denominator with respect to $n$):

$$\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{\frac{1}{n}}{1} = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n} = 0$$

Mathematical Meaning: Since the limit equals $0$, $n \log n$ is strictly dominated by $n^2$, denoted as $n \log n = o(n^2)$ (Little-o).

Empirical Comparison for Large $n$:

  • For $n = 10^6$: $n \log_2 n \approx 20 \times 10^6$ operations vs $n^2 = 10^{12}$ operations (a 50,000x difference!).
  • Hence, algorithms with $O(n \log n)$ complexity (e.g., Merge Sort) scale efficiently to millions of items, whereas $O(n^2)$ algorithms (e.g., Bubble Sort) become computationally infeasible.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: $\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{n \log n}{n^2} = 0$. $n \log n$ grows significantly slower than quadratic $n^2$. For $n=10^6$, $n \log n$ is 50,000 times faster than $n^2$.

title: Explain Strassen's Matrix Multiplication, including its seven recursive products.
answer_html:
Standard matrix multiplication of two $n \times n$ matrices requires $8$ recursive multiplications of size $n/2$, yielding $T(n) = 8T(n/2) + O(n^2) = O(n^{\log_2 8}) = O(n^3)$.

Strassen's Insight: Uses clever algebraic linear combinations to reduce multiplications from 8 down to 7.

For $2 \times 2$ block partitions $A = \begin{pmatrix} A_{11} & A_{12} \\ A_{21} & A_{22} \end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix} B_{11} & B_{12} \\ B_{21} & B_{22} \end{pmatrix}$, Strassen defines seven products:

  1. $P_1 = A_{11} (B_{12} - B_{22})$
  2. $P_2 = (A_{11} + A_{12}) B_{22}$
  3. $P_3 = (A_{21} + A_{22}) B_{11}$
  4. $P_4 = A_{22} (B_{21} - B_{11})$
  5. $P_5 = (A_{11} + A_{22}) (B_{11} + B_{22})$
  6. $P_6 = (A_{12} - A_{22}) (B_{21} + B_{22})$
  7. $P_7 = (A_{11} - A_{21}) (B_{11} + B_{12})$

Reconstructing the Result Matrix $C$:

  • $C_{11} = P_5 + P_4 - P_2 + P_6$
  • $C_{12} = P_1 + P_2$
  • $C_{21} = P_3 + P_4$
  • $C_{22} = P_1 + P_5 - P_3 - P_7$

Complexity Recurrence:

$$T(n) = 7T(n/2) + O(n^2) \implies T(n) = O(n^{\log_2 7}) \approx \mathbf{O(n^{2.807})}$$
simplified_html: Quick Recall: Reduces matrix multiplication from 8 to 7 subproblem multiplications using formulas $P_1..P_7$. Solves recurrence $T(n) = 7T(n/2) + O(n^2) = \mathbf{O(n^{2.807})}$, outperforming standard $O(n^3)$.

  • Subsequent occurrence of 'C' in $X$ is at index 5 (X[5] = 'C').

Since the complete sequence B -> D -> C appears intact in $X$ (at positions $X[1], X[4], X[5]$), the Longest Common Subsequence length is equal to the length of $Y$:

$$\mathbf{\text{Length of LCS} = 3, \quad \text{LCS} = \text{"BDC"}}$$

Tabulation (Bottom-Up Dynamic Programming): Computes values sequentially starting from base cases, storing each in a table to avoid redundant recursion.

Recurrence: $F(0) = 0, \, F(1) = 1, \, F(n) = F(n-1) + F(n-2)$ for $n \ge 2$.

Tabulation Array:

$n$Calculation$F(n)$
0Base case0
1Base case1
2$F(1) + F(0) = 1 + 0$1
3$F(2) + F(1) = 1 + 1$2
4$F(3) + F(2) = 2 + 1$3
5$F(4) + F(3) = 3 + 2$5
6$F(5) + F(4) = 5 + 3$8

Conclusion: $F(6) = \mathbf{8}$. Computed in $O(n)$ time and $O(n)$ space (or $O(1)$ space using two variables).
simplified_html: Quick Recall: Bottom-up table computes: $F(0)=0, F(1)=1, F(2)=1, F(3)=2, F(4)=3, F(5)=5, F(6)=8$. Avoids exponential recomputations in $O(n)$ time.

title: For edges A-B=3, A-C=2, C-B=5, B-D=2 and C-D=7, calculate the shortest distances from A using Dijkstra's algorithm.
answer_html:
Graph Specification: Vertices $V = \{A, B, C, D\}$, Source vertex $S = A$.

Edges: $(A, B) = 3, (A, C) = 2, (C, B) = 5, (B, D) = 2, (C, D) = 7$.

Step-by-Step Execution of Dijkstra's Algorithm:

  1. Initialization:
    • $dist = \{A: 0, B: \infty, C: \infty, D: \infty\}$
    • Visited set $S = \emptyset$.
  2. Step 1: Select unvisited vertex with min distance $\rightarrow$ $A$ ($dist=0$). $S = \{A\}$.
    • Relax neighbor $B$: $dist[B] = \min(\infty, 0 + 3) = 3$.
    • Relax neighbor $C$: $dist[C] = \min(\infty, 0 + 2) = 2$.
    • $dist = \{A: 0, B: 3, C: 2, D: \infty\}$.
  3. Step 2: Select min unvisited $\rightarrow$ $C$ ($dist=2$). $S = \{A, C\}$.
    • Relax neighbor $B$: $dist[B] = \min(3, 2 + 5) = 3$ (No change).
    • Relax neighbor $D$: $dist[D] = \min(\infty, 2 + 7) = 9$.
    • $dist = \{A: 0, B: 3, C: 2, D: 9\}$.
  4. Step 3: Select min unvisited $\rightarrow$ $B$ ($dist=3$). $S = \{A, B, C\}$.
    • Relax neighbor $D$: $dist[D] = \min(9, 3 + 2) = \mathbf{5}$ (Updated via path $A \to B \to D$).
    • $dist = \{A: 0, B: 3, C: 2, D: 5\}$.
  5. Step 4: Select min unvisited $\rightarrow$ $D$ ($dist=5$). $S = \{A, B, C, D\}$. All vertices visited.

Final Shortest Distances from A:

  • $A \to A$: $\mathbf{0}$
  • $A \to B$: $\mathbf{3}$ (Path: $A \to B$)
  • $A \to C$: $\mathbf{2}$ (Path: $A \to C$)
  • $A \to D$: $\mathbf{5}$ (Path: $A \to B \to D$)
simplified_html: Quick Recall: Dijkstra greedily settles vertices: $A(0) \to C(2) \to B(3) \to D(5)$. Shortest distances from A: $A=0, B=3, C=2, D=5$ (Path to D is $A \to B \to D$).

title: Explain the Floyd–Warshall algorithm and demonstrate how it updates an all-pairs distance matrix.
answer_html:
The Floyd-Warshall Algorithm is a Dynamic Programming algorithm that finds the shortest paths between all pairs of vertices in a directed, weighted graph (allowing negative edge weights, but no negative cycles).

Core DP Formulation:

Let $D^{(k)}[i, j]$ be the length of the shortest path from vertex $i$ to vertex $j$ using only intermediate vertices from the set $\{1, 2, \dots, k\}$.

$$D^{(k)}[i, j] = \min\left(D^{(k-1)}[i, j],\, D^{(k-1)}[i, k] + D^{(k-1)}[k, j]\right)$$

How the Matrix is Updated:

  1. Initialization ($D^{(0)}$): Direct edge weights from adjacency matrix ($D[i, i] = 0$, $D[i, j] = w(i, j)$, or $\infty$ if no direct edge).
  2. Iteration over $k = 1$ to $|V|$: At each phase $k$, vertex $k$ is considered as a potential intermediate waypoint. If travelling from $i$ to $k$ and then $k$ to $j$ is shorter than the currently recorded distance from $i$ to $j$, the matrix cell is updated.
  3. Final Matrix ($D^{(|V|)}$): Contains the true all-pairs shortest path distances.

Complexity: Three nested loops running $|V|$ times yield a time complexity of $\mathbf{\Theta(V^3)}$ and space complexity of $\Theta(V^2)$.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: All-Pairs Shortest Path via DP. Triple loop over intermediate node $k$: $D[i, j] = \min(D[i, j], D[i, k] + D[k, j])$. Time complexity $\Theta(V^3)$.

title: State two differences between an algorithm and a program.
answer_html:
Comparison between an Algorithm and a Program:

FeatureAlgorithmProgram
Design & LanguageAbstract, formal mathematical design written in pseudocode or natural language; completely independent of programming syntax or hardware.Concrete implementation written in a specific programming language (e.g., C, Java, Python) adhering to strict syntactic grammar.
ExecutionAnalyzed theoretically on paper (space/time complexity); cannot be executed directly by a computer CPU.Compiled or interpreted into machine instructions and executed directly on physical computer hardware.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: Algorithm = abstract, language-independent design (pseudocode). Program = concrete, machine-executable code written in a specific language (C, Java).

title: What is a stable sorting algorithm?
answer_html:
A sorting algorithm is defined as stable if two objects with equal keys appear in the same relative order in the sorted output as they appeared in the initial unsorted input array.

  • Formally, if $A[i] = A[j]$ and index $i < j$ in the input, then after sorting, the item originally at $i$ precedes the item originally at $j$.
  • Stable Sorts: Merge Sort, Insertion Sort, Bubble Sort, Counting Sort.
  • Unstable Sorts: Quick Sort, Heap Sort, Selection Sort.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: Preserves the original relative order of duplicate elements. Stable: Merge Sort, Insertion Sort. Unstable: Quick Sort, Heap Sort.

title: What is the purpose of a recurrence tree?
answer_html:
The purpose of a Recursion Tree is to provide a structured graphical visualization of the execution cost incurred at each recursive step of a divide-and-conquer recurrence relation:

  • Each node represents the non-recursive work performed at that subproblem ($f(n/b^i)$).
  • Summing the work horizontally across all nodes at each depth gives the per-level cost.
  • Summing the per-level costs vertically across all tree levels (from depth 0 to $\log_b n$) determines the total asymptotic time complexity, serving as an intuitive proof for the Master Theorem.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: Visualizes recursive calls as a tree. Horizontal sum gives cost per level; vertical sum over all levels gives total asymptotic complexity.

title: Define memoization.
answer_html:
Memoization is a top-down optimization technique in Dynamic Programming where the algorithm solves problems recursively, but before computing the solution to any subproblem, it checks a lookup cache (hash table or array):

  • If the subproblem has already been solved, its cached result is returned immediately ($O(1)$ lookup).
  • If not, the subproblem is computed recursively and its result is saved in the cache for future calls.
  • It maintains the intuitive structure of recursive code while eliminating exponential recomputations.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: Top-down DP approach: remembers recursive results in a table/cache so subproblems are never computed more than once.

title: What is a promising node in backtracking?
answer_html:
In Backtracking algorithms, a node in the state-space tree is called promising if it represents a partial solution that satisfies all problem constraints so far, meaning it has the potential to lead to a complete, valid solution.

  • Conversely, a non-promising node violates one or more bounding constraints; the algorithm immediately prunes that branch and backtracks without expanding its children.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: A state that does not violate constraints and can still lead to a valid solution. Non-promising nodes violate rules and are pruned immediately.

title: Differentiate between an upper bound and a tight asymptotic bound.
answer_html:
Comparison between Upper Bound and Tight Asymptotic Bound:

FeatureUpper Bound (Big-O, $O$)Tight Bound (Big-Theta, $\Theta$)
MeaningGuarantees that the running time does not exceed $c \cdot g(n)$ for large $n$. May or may not be tight.Guarantees that the running time grows at the exact same rate as $g(n)$, bounded both above and below.
Mathematical Condition$0 \le f(n) \le c \cdot g(n)$ for all $n \ge n_0$.$c_1 \cdot g(n) \le f(n) \le c_2 \cdot g(n)$ for all $n \ge n_0$.
Example ($f(n) = 3n + 2$)$f(n) = O(n)$ is valid, and $f(n) = O(n^2)$ is also mathematically valid (loose upper bound).Only $f(n) = \Theta(n)$ is valid; $f(n) \neq \Theta(n^2)$.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: Upper bound ($O$) is a ceiling that may be loose ($3n = O(n^2)$ is true). Tight bound ($\Theta$) matches the exact growth rate from both above and below ($3n = \Theta(n)$ only).

title: Explain why the dominant term is considered when determining asymptotic complexity.
answer_html:
When analyzing asymptotic complexity as input size $n \to \infty$:

  • The dominant term (the term with the highest degree or fastest mathematical growth rate) increases so rapidly that all lower-order terms and constant multipliers become mathematically negligible in comparison.
  • For example, in $f(n) = 0.001 n^2 + 1000 n$: for $n = 10^7$, the quadratic term contributes $10^{11}$ operations while the linear term contributes only $10^{10}$ operations (10% of total); as $n \to 10^9$, the quadratic term accounts for 99.9% of total time.
  • Hence, asymptotic analysis focuses solely on the dominant term to capture the true scalability of algorithms.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: As $n \to \infty$, the highest-order term grows so fast that lower-order terms become negligible. Dominant term determines the algorithm's true scalability.

title: State limitation of Counting Sort.
answer_html:
Two major limitations of Counting Sort are:

  • Range Sensitivity ($k$ must be small): The space complexity is $O(n + k)$ where $k$ is the range of values $(\max - \min)$. If $k = O(n^2)$ (e.g., sorting 10 numbers between 1 and 1,000,000), it requires an enormous array of 1 million integers, making it terribly inefficient in memory and time compared to comparison sorts.
  • Integer Restriction: It operates strictly on discrete non-negative integer keys (or objects mapped directly to small integers); it cannot sort floating-point real numbers or arbitrary unbounded strings directly.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: Limitations: (1) Inefficient when the value range $k$ is much larger than $n$ ($O(n+k)$ space). (2) Restricted to small non-negative integers; cannot directly sort floats or arbitrary text.

title: How many elements are placed in their final positions after one complete pass of Bubble Sort and Selection Sort?
answer_html:
After one complete pass over an unsorted array of size $n$:

  • Bubble Sort: Exactly one element (the global maximum element in ascending sort) is guaranteed to reach its final, permanent sorted position at the end of the array (index $n-1$).
  • Selection Sort: Exactly one element (the global minimum element in ascending sort) is selected and swapped into its final, permanent sorted position at the beginning of the array (index $0$).
simplified_html: Quick Recall: Exactly 1 element for both: Bubble Sort puts the maximum element at the end; Selection Sort puts the minimum element at the beginning.

title: Explain how divide and conquer is applied in large integer multiplication.
answer_html:
In Karatsuba's large integer multiplication (Divide and Conquer):

  1. Two $n$-digit integers $X$ and $Y$ are divided into high and low $n/2$-digit halves: $X = X_L \cdot 10^{n/2} + X_R$ and $Y = Y_L \cdot 10^{n/2} + Y_R$.
  2. Standard expansion requires 4 multiplications: $X_L Y_L, X_L Y_R, X_R Y_L, X_R Y_R$ ($O(n^2)$).
  3. Karatsuba's Divide-and-Conquer Trick: Computes only 3 recursive multiplications: $P_1 = X_L Y_L$, $P_2 = X_R Y_R$, and $P_3 = (X_L + X_R)(Y_L + Y_R)$. The middle cross-term is obtained via: $P_3 - P_1 - P_2$.
  4. This reduces time complexity to $T(n) = 3T(n/2) + O(n) = \mathbf{O(n^{\log_2 3}) \approx O(n^{1.585})}$.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: Karatsuba splits numbers into $n/2$ halves. Computes only 3 recursive multiplications instead of 4, reducing time from $O(n^2)$ down to $O(n^{1.585})$.

title: What is the worst-case time complexity of Quick Sort? Under what condition does it occur?
answer_html:
The worst-case time complexity of Quick Sort is $\mathbf{\Theta(n^2)}$ (Quadratic Time).

Conditions Under Which It Occurs:

  • Occurs when the partitioning routine produces the most unbalanced partitions possible: one subproblem with $n-1$ elements and one subproblem with $0$ elements at every recursive step.
  • Classic Scenario: When the input array is already sorted (in ascending or descending order) and the algorithm always picks the first or last element as the pivot.
  • Recurrence: $T(n) = T(n-1) + T(0) + \Theta(n) \implies T(n) = \Theta(n^2)$.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: Worst-case is $\mathbf{\Theta(n^2)}$. Occurs when the input is already sorted (or reverse sorted) and the pivot is chosen as the first/last element, producing $(n-1, 0)$ split.

title: Find an LCS of X = ABCBCABCAAB and Y = AC.
answer_html:
Strings: $X = \text{"ABCBCABCAAB"}$ ($m = 11$), $Y = \text{"AC"}$ ($n = 2$).

We check if the short string $Y = \text{"AC"}$ is a subsequence of $X$:

  • First character 'A' of $Y$ matches $X[0] = \text{'A'}$.
  • Second character 'C' of $Y$ matches $X[2] = \text{'C'}$ (which occurs after index 0).

Since the entire string $Y$ appears in order in $X$ (at indices 0 and 2), the Longest Common Subsequence is:

$$\mathbf{\text{LCS} = \text{"AC"}, \quad \text{Length} = 2}$$
simplified_html: Quick Recall: Both characters of $Y = \text{"AC"}$ appear in order within $X$ (at positions 0 and 2). Longest Common Subsequence is "AC" with length 2.

title: Given Huffman frequencies 4, 7, 8, 10 identify the first two combinations.
answer_html:
Huffman Algorithm Greedy Strategy: Repeatedly extract the two trees with the lowest frequencies from a priority queue (min-heap) and merge them into a new parent node whose frequency is the sum of both.

Initial Frequencies: $\{4, 7, 8, 10\}$

  1. Combination 1:
    • Extract the two smallest: $4$ and $7$.
    • Merge: Create parent node $N_1$ with frequency $= 4 + 7 = \mathbf{11}$.
    • Queue becomes: $\{8, 10, 11\}$.
  2. Combination 2:
    • Extract the two smallest from current queue: $8$ and $10$.
    • Merge: Create parent node $N_2$ with frequency $= 8 + 10 = \mathbf{18}$.
    • Queue becomes: $\{11, 18\}$.

Summary:

  • First Combination: 4 and 7 merged to form 11.
  • Second Combination: 8 and 10 merged to form 18.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: Huffman merges smallest pairs first: (1) Merge 4 and 7 -> 11. (2) From remaining {8, 10, 11}, merge 8 and 10 -> 18.

title: Explain why Rabin–Karp verifies the characters after finding equal hash values.
answer_html:
In the Rabin-Karp String Matching Algorithm, hash values are computed using modulo arithmetic (e.g., $hash \bmod q$, where $q$ is a prime number) to prevent arithmetic integer overflow.

Why character-by-character verification is required:

  • Because the hash range is finite ($0$ to $q-1$), two completely different strings can produce the exact same hash value. This phenomenon is known as a hash collision (or spurious hit).
  • Therefore, when the pattern hash matches the text window hash, the algorithm must verify each character one-by-one to confirm whether it is a genuine valid match or a false positive caused by a hash collision.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: Modulo arithmetic causes hash collisions (different strings having the same hash = spurious hit). Character-by-character verification confirms genuine matches vs false collisions.

title: What is a spurious hit and valid hit in Rabin–Karp string matching?
answer_html:
In Rabin-Karp String Matching:

  • Valid Hit: Occurs when the hash value of the text window matches the pattern hash ($hash(T[s..s+m-1]) == hash(P)$), AND subsequent character verification confirms that the characters are identical ($T[s..s+m-1] == P$). Represents a true occurrence of the pattern.
  • Spurious Hit: Occurs when the hash values match ($hash(T) == hash(P)$), BUT subsequent character verification reveals that the strings are actually different ($T[s..s+m-1] \neq P$). Caused by a mathematical hash collision resulting from modulo arithmetic.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: Valid hit = hash matches AND characters match (true match). Spurious hit = hash matches BUT characters differ (false positive collision).

title: Given two algorithms with time complexities T1(n) = 5n + 10 and T2(n) = n^2 + 2, determine for which values of n algorithm T1 is more efficient than T2.
answer_html:
To determine when $T_1(n)$ is more efficient than $T_2(n)$, solve for $T_1(n) < T_2(n)$:

$$5n + 10 < n^2 + 2 \implies n^2 - 5n - 8 > 0$$

Find the roots of the quadratic equation $n^2 - 5n - 8 = 0$ using the quadratic formula:

$$n = \frac{-(-5) \pm \sqrt{(-5)^2 - 4(1)(-8)}}{2(1)} = \frac{5 \pm \sqrt{25 + 32}}{2} = \frac{5 \pm \sqrt{57}}{2}$$

Since $\sqrt{57} \approx 7.55$:

$$n \approx \frac{5 + 7.55}{2} = \frac{12.55}{2} \approx 6.27$$

Conclusion:

  • For integer input sizes $n \ge 7$, $n^2 - 5n - 8 > 0$, meaning $T_1(n) < T_2(n)$.
  • Algorithm $T_1$ is strictly more efficient than $T_2$ for all $n \ge 7$. (For $n \le 6$, the quadratic algorithm $T_2$ is faster or equal due to smaller constants).
simplified_html: Quick Recall: Solving $5n + 10 < n^2 + 2$ yields $n > 6.27$. Algorithm $T_1$ is strictly more efficient than $T_2$ for all input sizes $n \ge 7$.

title:
Determine the time complexity of the following code:
for i = 1 to n
   for j = 1 to n
      k = k + 1
answer_html:
Given nested loop structure:

for i = 1 to n
   for j = 1 to n
      k = k + 1

Step-by-Step Analysis:

  1. The outer loop executes for $i = 1, 2, \dots, n$, running a total of $n$ iterations.
  2. For each iteration of the outer loop, the inner loop executes for $j = 1, 2, \dots, n$, running a total of $n$ iterations.
  3. Inside the inner loop, the statement k = k + 1 executes in constant $O(1)$ time.
  4. Total number of operations is given by the double summation:$$\sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} 1 = \sum_{i=1}^{n} n = n \times n = n^2$$

Time Complexity: $\mathbf{\Theta(n^2)}$ (Quadratic Time).
simplified_html: Quick Recall: Double nested loop where each loop runs $n$ times. Total operations $= n \times n = n^2$. Time complexity is $\mathbf{\Theta(n^2)}$.

title: For the array 29, 15, 34, 12, 27, 18 construct a max heap and show how the array is stored.
answer_html:
Initial Array: [29, 15, 34, 12, 27, 18] ($n = 6$)

A Max-Heap satisfies the property that every parent node is $\ge$ its children ($A[i] \ge A[2i+1]$ and $A[i] \ge A[2i+2]$).

Heapify Process (Bottom-Up from last non-leaf node index $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor - 1 = 2$):

  1. Index 2 (Value = 34): Left child at index 5 is 18. $34 > 18$, Heap property satisfied.
  2. Index 1 (Value = 15): Left child index 3 (12), Right child index 4 (27). Max child is 27. $15 < 27$, Swap 15 and 27.
    Subarray becomes: [29, 27, 34, 12, 15, 18]
  3. Index 0 (Value = 29): Left child index 1 (27), Right child index 2 (34). Max child is 34. $29 < 34$, Swap 29 and 34.
    Array becomes: [34, 27, 29, 12, 15, 18]
  4. Check index 2 (29) with its child index 5 (18): $29 > 18$, Heap property holds.

Final Max-Heap Array: $\mathbf{[34, 27, 29, 12, 15, 18]}$ (Root is 34; children of 34 are 27 and 29; children of 27 are 12 and 15; child of 29 is 18).
simplified_html: Quick Recall: Bottom-up heapify checks non-leaf nodes. Swaps (15, 27) and (29, 34). Final max-heap stored in array: [34, 27, 29, 12, 15, 18] with root 34.

title: Apply Insertion Sort to 3, 10, 23, 52, 49, 38, 56. Show the sorted portion after inserting 49 and 38.
answer_html:
Given Array: [3, 10, 23, 52, 49, 38, 56]

Initially, [3, 10, 23, 52] is already sorted.

  1. Pass inserting Key = 49:
    • Key 49 is compared with 52: $49 < 52$, shift 52 right.
    • Key 49 is compared with 23: $49 > 23$, insert 49 at index 3.
    • Sorted portion after inserting 49: [3, 10, 23, 49, 52]
  2. Pass inserting Key = 38:
    • Key 38 is compared with 52: shift 52 right.
    • Key 38 is compared with 49: shift 49 right.
    • Key 38 is compared with 23: $38 > 23$, insert 38 at index 3.
    • Sorted portion after inserting 38: [3, 10, 23, 38, 49, 52]
simplified_html: Quick Recall: Inserting 49 shifts 52: sorted portion is [3, 10, 23, 49, 52]. Inserting 38 shifts 52 and 49: sorted portion is [3, 10, 23, 38, 49, 52].

title: Explain Merge Sort using a suitable array and derive its recurrence relation.
answer_html:
Merge Sort is a recursive Divide-and-Conquer sorting algorithm with three phases:

  1. Divide: Computes the midpoint $q = \lfloor(p+r)/2\rfloor$ in $O(1)$ time.
  2. Conquer: Recursively sorts the two subarrays $A[p..q]$ and $A[q+1..r]$.
  3. Combine (Merge): Merges the two sorted subarrays in linear $O(n)$ time using a temporary array.

Example on [38, 27, 43, 3, 9, 82, 10]:

  • Splits into [38, 27, 43, 3] and [9, 82, 10].
  • Recursive merges yield left sorted [3, 27, 38, 43] and right sorted [9, 10, 82].
  • Final two-way merge produces: [3, 9, 10, 27, 38, 43, 82].

Recurrence Relation Derivation:

$$T(n) = \begin{cases} c & \text{if } n = 1 \\ 2T(n/2) + cn & \text{if } n > 1 \end{cases}$$

By Master Theorem (Case 2 with $a=2, b=2, f(n)=cn$ where $n^{\log_2 2} = n$):$$T(n) = \mathbf{\Theta(n \log n)}$$Merge Sort guarantees $\Theta(n \log n)$ time in all cases (best, worst, and average).
simplified_html: Quick Recall: Divides array into halves, recursively sorts, and merges in $O(n)$ time. Recurrence $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + cn$ solves to $\mathbf{\Theta(n \log n)}$ in all cases.

title: Consider an array [21, 3, 12, 17, 58, 1, 19, 18, 4, 15, 30]. Apply Min-Max Algorithm step by step and give the answer based on the algorithm.
answer_html:
Input: [21, 3, 12, 17, 58, 1, 19, 18, 4, 15, 30] ($n = 11$, indices 0..10)

Step-by-Step Divide-and-Conquer Execution:

  1. Divide at mid index 5: Left [21, 3, 12, 17, 58, 1] (0..5) and Right [19, 18, 4, 15, 30] (6..10).
  2. Left Subproblem (0..5):
    • Split 0..2: [21, 3, 12] $\rightarrow$ Min=3, Max=21.
    • Split 3..5: [17, 58, 1] $\rightarrow$ Min=1, Max=58.
    • Combine Left: $\min(3, 1) = \mathbf{1}$, $\max(21, 58) = \mathbf{58}$.
  3. Right Subproblem (6..10):
    • Split 6..7: [19, 18] $\rightarrow$ Min=18, Max=19.
    • Split 8..10: [4, 15, 30] $\rightarrow$ Min=4, Max=30.
    • Combine Right: $\min(18, 4) = \mathbf{4}$, $\max(19, 30) = \mathbf{30}$.
  4. Final Combine:$$\text{Global Minimum} = \min(\text{Left Min}, \text{Right Min}) = \min(1, 4) = \mathbf{1}$$$$\text{Global Maximum} = \max(\text{Left Max}, \text{Right Max}) = \max(58, 30) = \mathbf{58}$$

Final Answer: $\mathbf{\text{Minimum} = 1, \quad \text{Maximum} = 58}$.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: Left half minimum=1, maximum=58. Right half minimum=4, maximum=30. Final combine: $\mathbf{\text{Minimum} = 1, \text{Maximum} = 58}$.

title: Schedule jobs with deadline-profit pairs J1(3, 60), J2(2, 100), J3(3, 20), J4(1, 40), J5(2, 80) to maximize profit. Show the slot allocation.
answer_html:

Sort jobs in descending order of profit and greedily schedule each job in the latest available slot prior to its deadline.

  • $J_5$ (Profit 80, Deadline 2): Slot 2 occupied; next available slot $\le 2$ is Slot 1. Allocate $J_5 \rightarrow$ Slot 1.

title: Compare greedy algorithms and dynamic programming with respect to strategy, feasibility and optimal substructure.
answer_html:
Comparison between Greedy Algorithms and Dynamic Programming:

ParameterGreedy AlgorithmDynamic Programming
StrategyMakes the locally optimal choice at each step without ever reconsidering past choices (no backtracking).Evaluates all subproblem possibilities, solves overlapping subproblems once, and stores results in a table.
FeasibilityFast and intuitive ($O(n \log n)$ or $O(n)$), but does not guarantee optimality for all problem types (fails on 0/1 knapsack).Guarantees global optimality for any problem with optimal substructure, though computationally more intensive ($O(n^2)$ or $O(n \cdot W)$).
Optimal SubstructureRequired. The global optimum is formed by accumulating locally optimal greedy choices.Required. The global optimum is constructed from memoized/tabulated optimal solutions to overlapping subproblems.
Subproblem OverlapSubproblems do not need to overlap; greedy choice directly reduces the problem size.Strictly requires overlapping subproblems to realize efficiency gains.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: Greedy makes myopic local choices (never reconsiders; fast). DP exhaustively evaluates overlapping subproblems and guarantees global optimality via memoization/tabulation.

title: Consider a graph where a direct path exists: 1 -> 2 (weight 5), 2 -> 3 (weight 3), 1 -> 3 (weight 10). Show how the triangle inequality is checked and updated.
answer_html:
Triangle Inequality in Graph Theory: For any three vertices $u, v, w$, the shortest distance must satisfy: $dist(u, w) \le dist(u, v) + dist(v, w)$.

Given Edges:

  • Direct edge $(1, 3)$ with cost $= 10$.
  • Path via vertex 2: edge $(1, 2) = 5$ and edge $(2, 3) = 3$.

Checking Triangle Inequality:

  1. Calculate indirect path cost via intermediate vertex 2:$$dist(1, 2) + dist(2, 3) = 5 + 3 = \mathbf{8}$$
  2. Compare with direct path $dist(1, 3) = 10$:$$dist(1, 3) > dist(1, 2) + dist(2, 3) \quad (10 > 8)$$The triangle inequality is currently violated by the direct edge!
  3. Edge Relaxation / Matrix Update:$$\text{New } dist(1, 3) = \min(10, 5 + 3) = \mathbf{8}$$

The direct distance is relaxed and updated to 8 (using the path $1 \to 2 \to 3$), successfully satisfying the triangle inequality.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: Path $1 \to 2 \to 3$ costs $5 + 3 = 8$, which is shorter than direct edge $1 \to 3$ (cost 10). Relaxes $dist(1, 3)$ from 10 down to 8.

title: What is meant by the order of growth of an algorithm?
answer_html:
The Order of Growth (rate of growth) of an algorithm describes how its resource requirements (execution time or memory space) increase asymptotically as the input size $n$ approaches infinity.

  • It is obtained by focusing on the leading term of the exact time formula and ignoring constant coefficients and lower-order terms.
  • Common standard growth orders (from fastest to slowest): $O(1) < O(\log n) < O(n) < O(n \log n) < O(n^2) < O(n^3) < O(2^n) < O(n!)$.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: How runtime increases as input $n \to \infty$. Defined by the highest-order term (e.g., $O(1) < O(n) < O(n \log n) < O(n^2) < O(2^n)$).

title: State the worst-case and best-case time complexity of Bubble Sort.
answer_html:
Time complexity specifications for Bubble Sort:

  • Worst-Case Time Complexity: $\mathbf{\Theta(n^2)}$ (Quadratic Time). Occurs when the input array is sorted in reverse order; requires $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ comparisons and swaps.
  • Best-Case Time Complexity (Optimized with swapped flag): $\mathbf{\Theta(n)}$ (Linear Time). Occurs when the array is already sorted; the algorithm performs one pass of $n-1$ comparisons, detects zero swaps, and terminates immediately.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: Worst-case = $\mathbf{\Theta(n^2)}$ (reverse sorted array). Best-case = $\mathbf{\Theta(n)}$ (already sorted array with swap detection flag).

title: Define the combine step in divide and conquer.
answer_html:
In the Divide-and-Conquer paradigm, the Combine Step is the final phase where the algorithmic solutions derived independently from the smaller subproblems are synthesized and integrated together to construct the complete, correct solution for the original larger problem.

Example: In Merge Sort, the combine step is the two-way Merge() procedure that takes two already sorted sub-arrays and merges them into a single sorted array in linear $O(n)$ time.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: Merges/synthesizes solutions of subproblems into the final overall solution (e.g., the linear-time Merge() function in Merge Sort).

title: Define a longest common subsequence.
answer_html:
Given two sequences $X = \langle x_1, x_2, \dots, x_m \rangle$ and $Y = \langle y_1, y_2, \dots, y_n \rangle$, a sequence $Z = \langle z_1, z_2, \dots, z_k \rangle$ is a Common Subsequence if $Z$ is a subsequence of both $X$ and $Y$ (characters appear in the same relative order, but not necessarily contiguously).

A Longest Common Subsequence (LCS) is a common subsequence of maximum possible length $k$. It is computed via Dynamic Programming in $O(m \cdot n)$ time.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: The longest sequence of characters that appears in the same relative order (not necessarily consecutive) in both input strings.

title: What is a state-space tree in the N-Queens problem?
answer_html:
In the N-Queens problem, the State-Space Tree is a conceptual tree representation where:

  • The root node represents the initial state (an empty board with 0 queens placed).
  • Each level $k$ represents the decision of which column to place queen $k$ in row $k$.
  • Each branch corresponds to choosing a column $1, 2, \dots, N$.
  • Leaf nodes at depth $N$ represent complete configurations. Backtracking uses pruning functions to avoid generating dead-end subtrees where diagonal or column conflicts occur.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: A decision tree where each level represents placing a queen in a row, branches represent column choices, and paths from root to leaves represent candidate board solutions.

title: Explain Strassen's Matrix Multiplication using a 2 × 2 matrix example.
answer_html:
Let $A = \begin{pmatrix} a_{11} & a_{12} \\ a_{21} & a_{22} \end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix} b_{11} & b_{12} \\ b_{21} & b_{22} \end{pmatrix}$.

Instead of 8 scalar multiplications, Strassen computes 7 products:

  • $M_1 = (a_{11} + a_{22})(b_{11} + b_{22})$
  • $M_2 = (a_{21} + a_{22}) b_{11}$
  • $M_3 = a_{11} (b_{12} - b_{22})$
  • $M_4 = a_{22} (b_{21} - b_{11})$
  • $M_5 = (a_{11} + a_{12}) b_{22}$
  • $M_6 = (a_{21} - a_{11}) (b_{11} + b_{12})$
  • $M_7 = (a_{12} - a_{22}) (b_{21} + b_{22})$

The resulting product matrix $C = AB$ is formed by additions/subtractions:

  • $c_{11} = M_1 + M_4 - M_5 + M_7$
  • $c_{12} = M_3 + M_5$
  • $c_{21} = M_2 + M_4$
  • $c_{22} = M_1 - M_2 + M_3 + M_6$

Solving $T(n) = 7T(n/2) + O(n^2)$ yields $\mathbf{\Theta(n^{\log_2 7}) \approx \Theta(n^{2.807})}$.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: 7 intermediate products ($M_1..M_7$) replace 8 multiplications. Combines terms to yield 2x2 matrix $C$ in $\Theta(n^{2.807})$ time.

title: Explain how Randomized Quick Sort selects its pivot and why this can help avoid worst-case.
answer_html:
In Randomized Quick Sort, instead of deterministically picking a fixed index (like the first or last element), the pivot is chosen uniformly at random from the current subarray $A[p..r]$:

  1. Randomly select an index $k \in [p, r]$.
  2. Swap $A[k]$ with $A[r]$ (or $A[p]$).
  3. Execute standard partition around $A[r]$.

Why It Avoids the Worst-Case:

  • In standard Quick Sort, an adversary can deliberately supply an already sorted array to trigger worst-case $O(n^2)$ performance every single time.
  • With randomization, no particular input arrangement can consistently force unbalanced $(n-1, 0)$ splits. The algorithm guarantees an expected running time of $O(n \log n)$ for every possible input with high probability.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: Swaps a randomly selected index with the pivot position before partitioning. Prevents adversaries from crafting worst-case $O(n^2)$ sorted inputs, ensuring expected $O(n \log n)$ time.

title: Consider m=2, p=4, s=5, i=7. Generate Huffman Tree and calculate number of bits required to encode the message.
answer_html:
Given Characters and Frequencies: $m = 2, p = 4, s = 5, i = 7$. (Total characters $= 2 + 4 + 5 + 7 = 18$)

Step-by-Step Huffman Tree Construction:

  1. Min-heap contains: $\{(m, 2), (p, 4), (s, 5), (i, 7)\}$.
  2. Merge two smallest: $m(2)$ and $p(4) \rightarrow N_1(6)$ with left child $m$, right child $p$.
    Queue: $\{(s, 5), (N_1, 6), (i, 7)\}$.
  3. Merge two smallest: $s(5)$ and $N_1(6) \rightarrow N_2(11)$ with left child $s$, right child $N_1$.
    Queue: $\{(i, 7), (N_2, 11)\}$.
  4. Merge two remaining: $i(7)$ and $N_2(11) \rightarrow \text{Root}(18)$ with left child $i$, right child $N_2$.

Huffman Bit Codes (Left = 0, Right = 1):

  • $i$: 0 (Length = 1 bit)
  • $s$: 10 (Length = 2 bits)
  • $m$: 110 (Length = 3 bits)
  • $p$: 111 (Length = 3 bits)

Total Bits Calculation:

$$\text{Total Bits} = \sum (\text{frequency} \times \text{code length})$$$$\text{Total Bits} = (7 \times 1) + (5 \times 2) + (2 \times 3) + (4 \times 3) = 7 + 10 + 6 + 12 = \mathbf{35 \text{ bits}}$$
simplified_html: Quick Recall: Codes: $i=0$ (1 bit), $s=10$ (2 bits), $m=110$ (3 bits), $p=111$ (3 bits). Total encoded bits: $7(1) + 5(2) + 2(3) + 4(3) = \mathbf{35 \text{ bits}}$.

title: Why does Dijkstra's algorithm not work correctly for graphs containing negative edge weights? Explain with a suitable example.
answer_html:
Why Dijkstra Fails on Negative Edges:

  • Dijkstra's algorithm relies on a fundamental greedy property: once a vertex $u$ is extracted from the priority queue and added to the visited set $S$, its shortest path distance is assumed to be final and optimal.
  • If negative edges exist, a longer multi-edge path discovered later can have a negative total weight that is strictly shorter than the already settled path, violating the greedy assumption.

Counter-Example:

  • Consider vertices $A, B, C$ with edges: $(A, B) = 5$, $(A, C) = 2$, and $(C, B) = -4$.
  • Dijkstra settles $A (0)$, then relaxes $C (2)$ and $B (5)$.
  • Next, Dijkstra settles $C (2)$ as visited.
  • Next, it settles $B (5)$ as visited and permanently finalizes $dist[B] = 5$.
  • However, path $A \to C \to B$ has cost $2 + (-4) = \mathbf{-2}$, which is strictly less than $5$! Because $B$ was already marked visited, Dijkstra cannot update it, producing an incorrect distance.

Solution: Use the Bellman-Ford Algorithm for graphs with negative weights.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: Dijkstra assumes settled nodes never get shorter distances. Negative edges can create alternate paths that decrease settled distances (e.g., $A \to C \to B$ gives $-2$ vs direct $5$). Use Bellman-Ford instead.

title: Analyze the time complexity of sequential statements, selection statements and loops with suitable pseudocode examples.
answer_html:
Asymptotic time complexity analysis across basic programming control structures:

  1. Sequential Statements: Execute one after another. Total time is the sum of their individual execution times:$$T(n) = c_1 + c_2 + \dots + c_k = \mathbf{O(1)}$$
  2. Selection Statements (if-else): Evaluates a condition and executes one branch:$$T(n) = \text{Cost(Condition)} + \max(\text{Cost(Then-branch)}, \text{Cost(Else-branch)})$$Example: If the then branch runs an $O(n)$ loop and the else branch runs $O(1)$, worst-case complexity is $\mathbf{O(n)}$.
  3. Loops (for / while): Total time is the sum of costs across all iterations:$$T(n) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \text{Cost of body}(i)$$
    • Single Loop (1 to $n$): $n \times O(1) = \mathbf{O(n)}$.
    • Nested Loop ($1..n$ inside $1..n$): $n \times n = \mathbf{O(n^2)}$.
    • Logarithmic Loop ($i = i \times 2$): Halves or doubles problem size $\implies \mathbf{O(\log n)}$.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: Sequential = sum of constants $O(1)$; Selection = condition + max(branch) $O(\max)$; Loops = $\sum \text{body}$ (single loop $O(n)$, nested loop $O(n^2)$, doubling loop $O(\log n)$).

title: Compare the best-case, worst-case and average-case analysis of Linear Search.
answer_html:
Comprehensive analysis of Linear Search on array of $n$ elements:

  • Best-Case: The searched element is at the very first index $A[0]$. Algorithm executes exactly 1 comparison and halts. Time Complexity: $\mathbf{\Omega(1)}$.
  • Worst-Case: The searched element is at the last index $A[n-1]$ or absent from the array. Algorithm executes all $n$ comparisons. Time Complexity: $\mathbf{O(n)}$.
  • Average-Case: Assuming the element is equally likely to be at any index $i \in [1, n]$ with probability $1/n$:$$\text{Expected Comparisons} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} i \cdot \frac{1}{n} = \frac{1}{n} \cdot \frac{n(n+1)}{2} = \frac{n+1}{2}$$Time Complexity: $\mathbf{\Theta(n)}$ (Linear Time).
simplified_html: Quick Recall: Best-case: $\Omega(1)$ (1 comparison, index 0). Worst-case: $O(n)$ ($n$ comparisons, last/absent). Average-case: $\Theta(n)$ ($\frac{n+1}{2}$ comparisons).

title: Explain the Master Method and demonstrate how its three standard cases are used to solve recurrences.
answer_html:
The Master Method solves recurrences of the form:

$$T(n) = a T(n/b) + f(n) \quad \text{where } a \ge 1, b > 1$$

It compares $f(n)$ asymptotically with the critical function $n^{\log_b a}$:

  1. Case 1 ($f(n)$ grows polynomially slower than $n^{\log_b a}$):
    If $f(n) = O(n^{\log_b a - \epsilon})$ for some $\epsilon > 0$:$$T(n) = \mathbf{\Theta(n^{\log_b a})}$$Example: $T(n) = 8T(n/2) + 1000n^2$. $n^{\log_2 8} = n^3$. Since $n^2 = O(n^{3-1})$, $T(n) = \Theta(n^3)$.
  2. Case 2 ($f(n)$ and $n^{\log_b a}$ have the same order of growth):
    If $f(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_b a} \log^k n)$ for $k \ge 0$:$$T(n) = \mathbf{\Theta(n^{\log_b a} \log^{k+1} n)}$$Example: $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n$. $n^{\log_2 2} = n$. Here $f(n) = n = \Theta(n^1 \log^0 n) \implies T(n) = \Theta(n \log n)$.
  3. Case 3 ($f(n)$ grows polynomially faster and satisfies regularity):
    If $f(n) = \Omega(n^{\log_b a + \epsilon})$ for some $\epsilon > 0$ and $a f(n/b) \le c f(n)$ for $c < 1$:$$T(n) = \mathbf{\Theta(f(n))}$$Example: $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n^2$. $n^{\log_2 2} = n$. Since $n^2 = \Omega(n^{1+1})$, $T(n) = \Theta(n^2)$.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: Compares $f(n)$ with $n^{\log_b a}$. Case 1: tree leaves dominate $\implies \Theta(n^{\log_b a})$. Case 2: equal work per level $\implies \Theta(n^{\log_b a} \log n)$. Case 3: root dominates $\implies \Theta(f(n))$.

title: Explain the matrix-chain multiplication problem and show how the split position affects the number of scalar multiplications.
answer_html:
The Matrix Chain Multiplication Problem finds the optimal parenthesization of a product of $n$ matrices $A_1 A_2 \dots A_n$ that minimizes total scalar multiplications. Matrix multiplication is associative ($(AB)C = A(BC)$), but the parenthesization dramatically impacts operations.

Impact of Split Position $k$:

To multiply $A_{i..j}$, we choose an intermediate split point $k$ ($i \le k < j$) such that $(A_i \dots A_k)(A_{k+1} \dots A_j)$.

Recurrence: $m[i, j] = \min_{i \le k < j} \{m[i, k] + m[k+1, j] + p_{i-1} p_k p_j\}$.

Concrete Demonstration on 3 Matrices:

  • Dimensions: $A_1(10 \times 100), A_2(100 \times 5), A_3(5 \times 50)$.
  • Split at $k = 1$ ($(A_1(A_2 A_3))$): Cost $= (100 \times 5 \times 50) + (10 \times 100 \times 50) = 25,000 + 50,000 = \mathbf{75,000}$.
  • Split at $k = 2$ ($((A_1 A_2)A_3)$): Cost $= (10 \times 100 \times 5) + (10 \times 5 \times 50) = 5,000 + 2,500 = \mathbf{7,500}$.

Splitting at $k=2$ is 10 times faster than splitting at $k=1$, demonstrating the critical role of optimal parenthesization.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: Matrix multiplication is associative. Different parenthesization splits $k$ yield massive performance differences: $(A_1(A_2 A_3))$ costs 75,000 multiplications vs $((A_1 A_2)A_3)$ costing only 7,500 (10x reduction).

title: Explain how dynamic programming can solve the LCS problem. Illustrate the construction of the table using two short strings.
answer_html:
Dynamic Programming for Longest Common Subsequence (LCS):

Let $c[i, j]$ be the length of LCS for prefixes $X[1..i]$ and $Y[1..j]$.

Recurrence Formula:

$$c[i, j] = egin{cases} 0 & ext{if } i=0 ext{ or } j=0 \ c[i-1, j-1] + 1 & ext{if } X[i] == Y[j] \ \max(c[i-1, j], c[i, j-1]) & ext{if } X[i] eq Y[j] \end{cases}$$

Table Construction for $X = ext{"ABC"}$ and $Y = ext{"AC"}$:

$j=0$ ($\emptyset$)$j=1$ (A)$j=2$ (C)
$i=0$ ($\emptyset$)000
$i=1$ (A)01 ($ warrow$)1 ($\leftarrow$)
$i=2$ (B)01 ($\uparrow$)1 ($\uparrow$)
$i=3$ (C)01 ($\uparrow$)2 ($ warrow$)

Traceback: From cell $(3, 2) = 2$: $X[3] == Y[2] == ext{'C'} \implies$ record 'C', move to $(2, 1)$. Cell $(2, 1) = 1$ comes from $(1, 1)$. At $(1, 1)$, $X[1] == Y[1] == ext{'A'} \implies$ record 'A'.

LCS: $\mathbf{ ext{"AC"}}$ with Length = 2. Complexity: $\Theta(m \cdot n)$ time and space.
simplified_html: Quick Recall: Table of size $(m+1) \times (n+1)$. If characters match, $c[i, j] = 1 + c[i-1, j-1]$; if not, $\max(c[i-1, j], c[i, j-1])$. Traceback reconstructs LCS: "AC".

title: A salesperson needs to visit 4 cities (A, B, C, and D). They must start at City A, visit every other city exactly once, and return to City A. Find the route that minimizes total travel distance based on the given connections.
answer_html:
Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP) on 4 Cities $\{A, B, C, D\}$:

Distances from A: $AB=15, AC=18, AD=24$.
Distances from B: $BA=19, BC=37, BD=24$.
Distances from C: $CA=15, CB=35, CD=30$.
Distances from D: $DA=20, DB=25, DC=30$.

Starting and ending at city A, there are $(4-1)! = 3! = 6$ possible Hamiltonian tours:

  1. $A \to B \to C \to D \to A$: Cost $= 15 + 37 + 30 + 20 = \mathbf{102}$
  2. $A \to B \to D \to C \to A$: Cost $= 15 + 24 + 30 + 15 = \mathbf{84}$
  3. $A \to C \to B \to D \to A$: Cost $= 18 + 35 + 24 + 20 = \mathbf{97}$
  4. $A \to C \to D \to B \to A$: Cost $= 18 + 30 + 25 + 19 = \mathbf{92}$
  5. $A \to D \to B \to C \to A$: Cost $= 24 + 25 + 35 + 15 = \mathbf{99}$
  6. $A \to D \to C \to B \to A$: Cost $= 24 + 30 + 35 + 19 = \mathbf{108}$

Optimal Tour:

$$\mathbf{A \to B \to D \to C \to A \quad \text{with minimum total distance } = \mathbf{84 \text{ km}}}$$
simplified_html: Quick Recall: Evaluates all 6 possible Hamiltonian cycles starting from A. The minimum cost tour is $\mathbf{A \to B \to D \to C \to A}$ with total travel distance of $\mathbf{84 \text{ km}}$.

title: Given a Text T and a Pattern P: Text (T): A C A A B C B B A A B; Pattern (P): A A B. Tasks: 1. Find all valid shifts where the pattern occurs in the text. 2. Calculate the total number of character-to-character comparisons performed by the algorithm.

  5. $s = 4$ ("BCB"): $P[0]='A' eq T[4]='B'$ (1). Mismatch! $ ightarrow$ 1 comparison.
  6. $s = 5$ ("CBB"): $P[0]='A' eq T[5]='C'$ (1). Mismatch! $ ightarrow$ 1 comparison.
